ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**1:** Both sections argue that a single LLM call cannot handle complex problems the way a multi-step system can, and both preview the same four patterns. The generated section's version of this argument is thinner than the expected section's 'black box' framing and has no personal anecdote, but the core substantive claim is present.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** Both sections argue single complex prompts are hard to debug (both explicitly use the phrase 'black box'), lack modularity, suffer from lost-in-the-middle, and degrade in reliability (the same 52.9% error-rate statistic), and both walk through the identical FAQ example. As in every article graded, the phrasing-sensitivity and context-overflow points have no clean standalone counterpart, treated as tolerable compression. Notably, this section also explains *why* lost-in-the-middle happens (causal attention masking and positional encoding decay) in more theoretical detail than the expected section, which only describes the phenomenon -- see DepthEnhancement below.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** All four of the guideline's clearly-named benefits are present (modularity, accuracy, debugging, flexibility with the cheap/expensive-model example, here labeled 'specialization'). Cost/latency and information-loss/cascading-failure are both explicit; the distinct 'instructions lose their meaning when split' point and the 'glue code' point have no separate counterpart, treated as tolerable compression.

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections build the identical 3-step chain, combine it into a sequential_workflow function, and measure the same 22.20-second execution time. As in another article graded, the corrected-output example is a tight match to the expected section's own illustration, both specifically naming 'Understanding Wind Turbines' and 'Energy Storage Solutions' as the two sources the fixed pipeline correctly attributes.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections explain the independence of answering/sourcing, build the same async function pair and asyncio.gather-based parallel_workflow, report the same 22.20s-to-8.98s speedup, cover the sequential-vs-parallel trade-off, and include a rate-limit caution (backoff with jitter) at the section's close.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**1:** The core ideas -- fixed workflows can't adapt, an LLM call as classifier, divide-and-conquer, and a customer-service illustration -- are all present, and the expected section's model-routing callout is satisfied by the cost-optimization/cheaper-model routing point. The section additionally goes into substantial, well-sourced breadth (a decision-tree analogy, and industry applications in finance and content operations) not present in the expected section -- see BreadthEnhancement below.

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections implement the identical IntentEnum/UserIntent classification model, the same classify_intent function, the same three specialized prompts, and the same handle_query router. As with every other article graded under this guideline, the expected section's paragraph on intent-classification best practices (taxonomy design, examples for edge cases, a two-stage retrieve-then-classify architecture) has no counterpart -- the added content here (ambiguous/compound-intent failure modes, and when a rule engine beats an LLM classifier) is genuinely valuable (see DepthEnhancement below) but addresses a different question, so CoreContent still fails on that missing idea cluster.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**0:** Both sections define the orchestrator-worker pattern the same way, frame its flexibility/dynamic-nature advantage identically, and walk through the same three-issue customer query with matching schemas. However, per standing ruling, this section never addresses API rate limiting as a real-world limitation of this pattern, despite it dispatching multiple LLM calls per query -- a confirmed omission that fails CoreContent on its own. Separately, the main pipeline function (process_user_query) that ties the orchestrator, workers, and synthesizer together is never shown at all, not even abbreviated -- the code jumps straight from defining the individual pieces to calling a function that was never defined, a gap beyond what the expected section's own aside (which only omits the worker internals) accounts for.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections recap the same four patterns and close by connecting the lesson to the broader practice of AI engineering and previewing what's next. The next-lesson preview covers the same theme (tools/function calling) without a specific lesson number, which per established precedent is a guideline_adherence matter, not a CoreContent one.
